source_text: Καὶ μὴ τοῦθ', ὅπερ εἶδος διαλεκτικὴ κατορθοῦν μόνη εἴληχε. τὸ δέ γε πάλιν ταπεινὸν τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῶν, ἐκτεθαμβημένων μὲν τῇ μεγαλουργίᾳ καὶ θαυματουργίᾳ καὶ ποικίλῃ καὶ πανσόφῳ δημιουργίᾳ τῇ τοῦ κόσμου, καὶ τεθαυμακότων μὲν ἀλόγως, ὑποπτηκότων δὲ ὑπὸ ἐκπλήξεως· εἰδότων δὲ οὔθ' ὁτιοῦν ἐπιλογίσασθαι δίκην ἀλόγων ζώων, ἐξεγείρων καὶ ἀνορθῶν μαθήμασιν ἑτέροις τοῖς φυσικοῖς· σαφηνίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ὄντων καὶ διακρίνων, καὶ μάλα σοφῶς εἰς τὰ πρώτιστα στοιχεῖα κατεπιπλέκων τῷ λόγῳ, καὶ ἐπιπορευόμενος τήν τε τῶν ὅλων καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ μέρους ἑκάστου φύσιν, τροπήν τε τὴν πολυειδῆ καὶ μεταβολὴν τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ· ἕως φέρων ὑπὸ σαφοῦς τῆς παρ' αὐτοῦ διδασκαλίας καὶ λόγων, ὧν τε ἔμαθεν ὧν τε ἐξεύρετο περὶ τῆς τῶν ὅλων οἰκονομίας τῆς ἱερᾶς καὶ φύσεως τῆς ἀμωμήτου, ἀντὶ ἀλόγου λογικὸν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν ἐγκατέθετο θαῦμα. τοῦθ' ὃ δὴ μάθημα ὑψηλὸν καὶ ἔνθεον ὄν, ἡ ἐρασμιωτάτη πᾶσιν ἐκδιδάσκει φυσιολογία. τί δεῖ λέγειν τὰ τῶν ἱερῶν μαθημάτων, γεωμετρίαν μὲν τὴν πᾶσι φίλην καὶ ἀναμφισβήτητον, καὶ ἀστρονομίαν τὴν μετεωροπόρον; ἃ δὴ ἕκαστα ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν ἐνετυποῦτο διδάσκων, ἢ ἀναμιμνήσκων, ἢ οὐκ οἶδ' ὅ,τι χρὴ λέγειν· τὴν μέν, ὡς ὑποβάθραν πάντων ἁπλῶς ποιησάμενος οὖσαν ἄσειστον, τὴν γεωμετρίαν, καὶ κρηπῖδα τινὰ ἀσφαλῆ· ἀνάγων δὲ καὶ μέχρι τῶν ἀνωτάτω διὰ τῆς ἀστρονομίας, ὥσπερ διὰ κλίμακός τινος οὐρανομήκους ἑκατέρου τοῦ μαθήματος, βατὸν ἡμῖν τὸν οὐρανὸν παρασκευάσας.
orientation: Origen leads them through natural science, geometry and astronomy toward the highest things.
pass_a_gloss: And not this [only], which kind dialectic alone has been allotted to set right. But again the lowly [part] of our soul, of [us] astounded at the great-working and wonder-working and varied and all-wise craftsmanship of the world, and having wondered irrationally, and cowering from astonishment, and knowing not anything to reckon after the manner of irrational animals; rousing and setting upright by other studies, the natural; making clear each of the beings and distinguishing, and very wisely weaving down by the argument into the very first elements, and going through the nature of the wholes and of each in part, and the many-formed turning and change of things in the world; until, bearing [us] by the clear teaching and arguments from him, both those he learned and those he discovered, about the sacred economy of the wholes and blameless nature, he deposited in our souls instead of irrational a rational wonder. This which [is] a lofty and divine study, the most lovely to all, natural philosophy, teaches. What need to say the things of the sacred studies: geometry, dear to all and indisputable, and astronomy, the sky-traversing? Which each he imprinted on our souls, teaching, or reminding, or I know not what one should say: the one, geometry, making it simply the base of all, being unshaken, and some safe foundation; and leading up even to the highest things through astronomy, as through some heaven-high ladder, by each of the two studies, having prepared heaven passable for us.

pass_b_english: And he did not train only that part which it falls to dialectic alone to set right. There was also the lowly part of our soul. We were awestruck at the mighty works and marvels and the varied, all-wise craftsmanship of the world; we marveled without reason and cowered in astonishment, and like animals without reason we did not know how to reason about any of it at all. This part he roused and set upright by other studies, those of nature. He made clear each thing that exists and distinguished it, and with great wisdom worked his account down to the very first elements; he went through the nature of the whole and of each part, and the many kinds of turning and change in the things of the world. At last, carrying us along by his clear teaching and by the arguments, both those he had learned and those he had found out for himself, about the sacred ordering of the universe and its blameless nature, he set in our souls a reasoned wonder in place of an unreasoning one. Natural science, which all find most delightful, teaches this lofty and divine study.

Why should I speak of the sacred studies, geometry, dear to all and beyond dispute, and astronomy, which travels the heights? He stamped each of these on our souls, by teaching them, or by reminding us of them, or I do not know what I ought to call it. Geometry he made the unshakable base of absolutely everything, a sure foundation; and through astronomy he led us up to the highest things, making heaven passable for us by each of the two studies, as by a ladder reaching up to heaven.
notes: The first sentence also closes the source row of 7.2; it is translated here only, where Koetschau begins chapter 8 and where the grammar carries it (it introduces 'the lowly part of our soul'). The verb of that long sentence is the participle 'rousing', so the English supplies 'he did not train only' and 'This part he roused' to make the sentence readable; no idea is added. 'A ladder reaching up to heaven' (κλίμακος οὐρανομήκους) may recall Jacob's ladder (Genesis 28:12), but the wording differs and the image was also common in philosophy, so it is not cited. 'Reminding us' (ἀναμιμνήσκων) alludes to the Platonic idea that learning is recollection; not Scripture. Readings: κατορθοῦν (print; Koetschau κατορθοῖν); οὔθ᾽ ὁτιοῦν (print); κατεπιπλέκων (print), rendered 'worked his account down to the very first elements' (Koetschau punctuates 'distinguishing them into the first elements, and weaving them together'); μάλα σοφῶς and σαφοῦς are read with Koetschau where the print's ligatures are unclear at scan resolution; ἁπλῶς ('absolutely', print); ἐνετυποῦτο ('stamped', print). Ends at παρασκευάσας; section 9 begins with ethics.
